summary: This document discusses the security implications of native IPv6 support and IPv6 transition mechanisms on networks that are thought of as IPv4-only. It also describes possible mitigations. Even if you never turned IPv6 on, devices may still speak it.

plainLanguage.summary: Locking your front door does not help if a hidden side door is open. Even a building that thinks it only has one door may have another one, and this explains how to lock it.

subtitle: Why a network that thinks it is IPv4-only can still be attacked over IPv6, and how to filter it.

tldr.problem: Most operating systems enable IPv6 and several transition technologies by default, so enterprise networks meant to be IPv4-only can be reached or attacked over IPv6 in ways their IPv4 controls do not see.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC applies the same security policies to native IPv6 and tunneled IPv6 as to IPv4, or blocks that traffic, and lists concrete filtering rules for each tunneling mechanism.
tldr.outcome: Filtering IPv6 is described as a temporary measure until IPv6 is properly deployed, and the RFC warns that blocking it can cause slow fallbacks to IPv4.

today: RFC 7123 is an Informational RFC published in February 2014 and has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata. Its advice is aimed at enterprise networks and is framed as a temporary measure until IPv6 is deployed.

sections.title: The Problem: Unplanned IPv6
sections.content:
Most general-purpose operating systems enable native IPv6 and a number of transition technologies by default. Some enterprise networks choose to delay active use of IPv6, and this RFC covers the security exposure that results from unplanned IPv6 use there. It applies only to enterprise networks, not to home networks or to provider networks such as ISPs.

The RFC lists several ways this goes wrong. A network intrusion detection system (NIDS) may know IPv4 attack patterns but miss the same attack carried over a tunnel. An IPv4 firewall may not enforce the same policy for IPv6. Some mechanisms, notably Teredo, can make an internal host reachable from the Internet over IPv6. IPv6-unaware VPN software on a dual-stack host can also leak traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer may speak a second language that your security guard does not understand. Someone can use that second language to sneak past the guard.

sections.title: Native IPv6 and How to Filter It
sections.content:
Because IPv6 is usually on by default, hosts on an "IPv4-only" network are likely to have at least link-local IPv6 connectivity. An attacker on the local network could also impersonate a router by sending Router Advertisement messages, which makes hosts enable their non-link-local IPv6 connectivity and may bypass controls that only covered IPv4.

The preferred answer is to enforce on IPv6 the same policies enforced on IPv4, for example with an IPv6-enabled NIDS and IPv6 firewalling. Where that is not feasible, layer-2 devices may block Ethernet frames with the Protocol Type field set to 0x86dd. The RFC cautions that this can cause hard-to-diagnose problems, such as breaking link-local uses like Multicast DNS. RA-Guard helps against SLAAC-based attacks and DHCPv6-Shield against DHCPv6-based ones, but neither stops attacks that use link-local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The best fix is to teach the guard the new language. If that is too hard, you can shut the side door, but then some things that used it will stop working.

sections.title: Tunneling and the Default-Deny Approach
sections.content:
Tunneling mechanisms can increase host exposure, be used to evade security controls, and contain vulnerabilities or bugs. Automatic tunneling mechanisms such as Teredo, ISATAP and 6to4 are of particular interest because they can be used without the consent of the user or administrator. The RFC recommends a default deny policy: transition traffic is blocked unless someone explicitly decides to allow it. It also recommends disabling these mechanisms on each node, in addition to filtering at the organizational perimeter.

Most IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnels can be blocked by dropping IPv4 packets whose Protocol field is 41. This covers 6in4, 6over4, 6rd, 6to4 and ISATAP. The RFC says such filtering belongs on the network that is the target of the traffic, and that transit traffic, for instance at an ISP, should generally never be filtered.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of guessing which doors are safe, keep every door shut by default and open one only when you decide to. You should also nail shut the doors on each room.

sections.title: Filtering Rules for Specific Mechanisms
sections.content:
When only some tunnels should be blocked, finer rules exist. For 6to4, filter IPv4 packets to or from 192.88.99.0/24, or, if the device can inspect the payload, packets with Protocol 41 carrying IPv6 addresses in 2002::/16. For 6over4, block Protocol 41 packets destined to 239.0.0.0/8.

Teredo clients must contact a Teredo server on UDP port 3544, so an organizational firewall can filter outgoing UDP to that port. The RFC notes this does not stop an attacker who runs a server on another port, and a host might still reach some Teredo peers without any server. Tunnel Broker with TSP uses port 3653 over TCP and UDP. AYIYA, whose specification was never published as an RFC, uses port 5072. ISATAP is hard to block by name resolution, because Windows finds its router through DNS and LLMNR names.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of secret passage has its own knock and its own door. The RFC lists which door to watch for each one.

sections.title: Side Effects of Filtering IPv6
sections.content:
Many hosts prefer IPv6 whenever it seems available. If a host believes it has IPv6 connectivity but the path fails upstream, it may wait a non-trivial time before falling back to IPv4, depending on how Happy Eyeballs is implemented. For this reason the RFC suggests that networks blocking IPv6 configure local recursive DNS servers to answer AAAA queries with RCODE 0 (NOERROR) or ignore them, so hosts only see A records.

That approach has a drawback with DNSSEC: stripping AAAA records makes responses to queries with the DO and CD bits set be considered invalid. The RFC also advises signaling drops to the source, for example with an ICMPv6 error or a TCP RST segment, so the sender can react quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: If you close a door without telling anyone, people keep knocking and waiting. It is kinder and faster to put up a sign that says the door is closed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own security section is short. The possible mitigations boil down to enforcing on native IPv6 and IPv6 transition traffic the same security policies enforced for IPv4, or blocking that traffic when it is deemed undesirable.

The RFC also says that filtering IPv6 to protect IPv4 networks should generally be considered only a temporary measure until IPv6 is deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Either give the new door the same lock as the old one, or board it up until you are ready to use it.
